issues.legal_issue: A market fee is valid only when a substantial portion of the collections is used to provide a special, reasonably correlated benefit to those who bear the fee in connection with the regulated transactions.
material_facts: The fee was collected from buyers of agricultural produce, principally traders licensed to operate in notified market areas.
The dealers challenged increases in the fee on the ground that the services and expenditure were not sufficiently connected to the fee payers and their purchase transactions.
The authorities’ duty to show the required correlation could be assessed broadly and reasonably, rather than with mathematical precision.
issues.conclusion: A market fee must be supported by a substantial, reasonably ascertainable quid pro quo: a good and substantial portion of its proceeds must be spent on services that directly and reasonably benefit fee payers in relation to the transactions for which the fee is imposed.
issues.legal_principle: The distinction between a tax and a fee, and the requirement of quid pro quo for this kind of fee, were drawn from The Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras v. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar of Sri Shirur Mutt; The Hingir-Rampur Coal Co. Ltd. v. State of Orissa; Indian Mica & Micanite Industries Ltd. v. State of Bihar; and the other authorities reviewed in the judgment. A fee need not be matched to services with arithmetical exactitude, but the services must provide a special benefit to the payer and relate to the relevant transaction; remote or indirect benefits to traders are insufficient. A good and substantial portion of the collections must be shown, with reasonable certainty, to be spent on such services.

rule.if: market_fee_challenge and fee_burden_falls_on_identifiable_payers and (substantial_proceeds_not_shown_for_transaction_related_services or only_remote_benefit_shown)

predicates.market_fee_challenge: A party challenges a levy imposed as a market fee.
predicates.fee_burden_falls_on_identifiable_payers: The fee is imposed on an identifiable person or class of persons in connection with specified transactions.
predicates.substantial_proceeds_not_shown_for_trans: The authority has not shown with reasonable certainty that a good and substantial portion of the collections is spent on services for the fee payers related to those transactions.
predicates.only_remote_benefit_shown: The claimed benefit to fee payers is only indirect or remote, such as a general increase in agricultural production that may eventually increase market transactions.

issues.definition: When a challenged market fee is imposed on identifiable payers, it is invalid if a substantial portion of the proceeds is not shown to fund transaction-related services or the claimed benefit is only remote.

issues.legal_issue: Market-fee proceeds may be used only for services and facilities sufficiently connected to transactions in the market, not for general agricultural, village-development, or public purposes.
material_facts: The statutory funds received market-fee proceeds and could be spent on enumerated purposes under the governing legislation.

The authorities had used, or proposed to use, substantial sums for items including village link roads, agricultural production and improvement, village electrification, and facilities intended mainly for agriculturists.
The judgment distinguished market facilities and access serving the market from works or assistance extending across villages or the wider market area for general agricultural benefit.
The Court held that the provisions listing expenditure purposes could be applied subject to limits on the use of market-fee proceeds, without striking those provisions down as unconstitutional.
issues.conclusion: Market-fee proceeds may fund services and facilities connected with marketing transactions and special benefits to traders, including qualifying facilities in or serving the market. They may not fund general agricultural improvement, village facilities or roads remote from the market, or other general or public purposes; the statutory expenditure provisions were restricted accordingly rather than struck down.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 26 and 28 of the Punjab Agricultural Produce Markets Act, 1961, governed expenditure from the Marketing Development Fund and Market Committee Fund. Read with sections 25, 27, and 32, their purposes could be funded from market-fee collections only insofar as they served market transactions and provided the required special benefit to fee payers. The Court treated market facilities and approach works serving a market differently from general village roads and agricultural improvement. Its analysis applied the quid pro quo principles from Shirur Mutt, Hingir-Rampur Coal Co., and Indian Mica & Micanite Industries Ltd. The Court restricted the operation of the expenditure provisions instead of declaring them constitutionally invalid.

predicates.market_fee_fund_use_challenge: A party challenges the use of a fund containing market-fee proceeds.
predicates.expenditure_funded_from_market_fees: The authority uses or proposes to use proceeds collected as market fees to pay for an expenditure.
predicates.expenditure_serves_general_agriculture_o: The expenditure serves general agricultural, village-development, or public interests rather than providing facilities or services connected to market transactions.

issues.definition: If a challenged expenditure is paid from market-fee proceeds but serves general agricultural or public interests rather than market transactions, those proceeds cannot fund it.

issues.legal_issue: A marketing board may fix the market-fee rate for market committees when the governing scheme subjects the committees’ levy to rules and gives the board supervisory control over them.
material_facts: The legislation authorised market committees to levy fees subject to rules made by the State Government.
A rule provided for the rate to be fixed by the marketing board from time to time, within the legislative maximum.
The legislation gave the board superintendence and control over the committees.
The dealers argued that the board’s fixing of the rate amounted to an unlawful abdication of the committees’ function.
issues.conclusion: The board’s power under the rule to fix the rate from time to time within the legislative maximum was not ultra vires; the committees were required to follow the rate fixed by the board.
issues.legal_principle: Section 23 of the Punjab Agricultural Produce Markets Act, 1961, made the committee’s power to levy fees subject to rules. Rule 29 assigned rate-fixing within the statutory maximum to the board, while section 3(9) conferred superintendence and control over committees. In this statutory context, that supervisory power supported the rule. State of Punjab v. Hari Krishan Sharma was distinguished because the legislation in that case did not make the relevant licensing power subject to a rule conferring overriding control of this kind.

rule.if: market_fee_rate_setting_challenge and committee_levy_is_subject_to_rules and board_has_superintendence_over_committees and board_rate_remains_within_legislative_maximum

predicates.market_fee_rate_setting_challenge: A party challenges the authority to set the rate of a market fee.
predicates.committee_levy_is_subject_to_rules: The governing scheme makes a committee’s power to levy the fee subject to rules.
predicates.board_has_superintendence_over_committee: The governing scheme gives a board superintendence and control over the committees.
predicates.board_rate_remains_within_legislative_ma: The board fixes the rate within the maximum set by the legislature.

issues.definition: The board may validly set the fee rate when the committee’s levy is subject to rules, the board supervises the committees, and the rate remains within the legislative maximum.

issues.legal_issue: An increase in market fees must be justified by expenditure on legally permissible services, and the record did not justify the challenged increase beyond the previously sustained level.
material_facts: The committees and boards had undertaken substantial development work in the markets, and the Court took a reasonable and practical view of the material before it in sustaining the fee at the previously upheld level.
The authorities relied on general agricultural and village-development works, including link roads, as grounds for increasing the fee.

The material showed that a substantial share of expenditure was directed to purposes not sufficiently connected to market transactions, and the authorities had acted on the mistaken view that fee proceeds could be spent on any development work in the market area.
The record did not provide an adequate, properly prepared overall account of funds, income, and projected expenditure to justify the further increase.
issues.conclusion: The fee at the previously sustained level was upheld, but the further increase was invalid on the record because it was chiefly justified by expenditure that could not lawfully be financed from market-fee proceeds. Any further increase would require reliable budgets, estimates, and accounts establishing a reasonable basis for it.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 23 of the Punjab Agricultural Produce Markets Act, 1961, the fee was subject to a legislative maximum, but the validity of a particular rate also depended on the fee principles developed in Shirur Mutt, Hingir-Rampur Coal Co., and Indian Mica & Micanite Industries Ltd. A higher rate could not be justified by treating fee collections as general revenue for development or agricultural welfare. The Court assessed the evidence practically, sustained the existing level in light of market development already undertaken, and found the further increase unsupported by legally permissible expenditure and adequate financial materials.

predicates.market_fee_increase_challenge: A party challenges an increase in a market fee.
predicates.increase_relies_on_ineligible_general_de: The authority justifies the increase chiefly by spending on general agricultural, village, or other development purposes that are not sufficiently connected to market transactions.
predicates.substantial_fee_proceeds_not_shown_for_m: The authority has not shown that a good and substantial portion of the fee proceeds is spent on permissible market services.
predicates.reliable_financial_estimates_do_not_supp: Reliable budgets, estimates, and accounts do not establish that the proposed increase is justified by expected permissible expenditure.

issues.definition: A challenged fee increase is invalid when it relies on ineligible general development spending and the record does not establish sufficient permissible market expenditure or reliable financial support for the increase.
